parsed.wine_summary:
Shafer is one of the defining producers of Stags Leap District, with roots going back to 1972 when John Shafer bought a hillside property that would become some of Napa's most prized Cabernet vineyards. One Point Five launched in 2003 as a way to offer estate-grown Stags Leap District Cabernet at a more accessible price than Hillside Select, which routinely sells for $300+. The wine is predominantly Cabernet Sauvignon with small amounts of Merlot and Petit Verdot blended in depending on the vintage.

What makes One Point Five worth paying attention to is the sourcing. These are estate vineyards on volcanic tuff and Bale clay loam — the same soil types that give Stags Leap District its signature combination of power and texture. The Palisades rock formation to the east casts an afternoon shadow over the vineyards, pulling temperatures down during the critical ripening hours. This diurnal swing preserves acidity while allowing full phenolic ripeness, which is why Stags Leap Cabernets tend to have rounder, more integrated tannins than wines from Oakville or Rutherford at similar concentration levels.
parsed.terroir_expression: Stags Leap District's volcanic tuff soils — porous, mineral-dense, and well-drained — force vine roots deep into fractured bedrock, concentrating flavors and adding a faint iron-mineral undercurrent to the fruit. The AVA sits in a natural amphitheater formed by the Vaca Mountains, which traps daytime heat but channels cool evening air through a gap in the hills, creating a thermal inversion pattern that extends the growing season without baking the grapes. In One Point Five, this translates to dark fruit that stays lifted rather than jammy, tannins that feel polished rather than aggressive, and a mid-palate density that carries a subtle rocky, almost graphite-like minerality. The valley floor and lower hillside sites contributing to this wine have deeper alluvial deposits mixed with the volcanic base, which adds flesh and generosity compared to the leaner, more austere hillside-only Hillside Select.
parsed.vinification_summary: Shafer ferments in stainless steel tanks with extended maceration — meaning the juice stays in contact with grape skins well after fermentation finishes, extracting additional tannin, color, and flavor compounds in a controlled way. The wine then ages in French oak barrels, typically around 20 months, with a significant percentage of new oak. This oak regimen adds vanilla, baking spice, and a cedary framework without overwhelming the fruit, partly because the base material is concentrated enough to absorb it. Shafer was an early adopter of solar-powered winemaking operations and uses 100% estate fruit, giving them complete control from vine to bottle — a meaningful distinction in Napa, where many high-end labels source grapes from multiple vineyards across the valley.
